title: The schedule mirrors the team
subtitle: Why functional project managers build functional schedules — and what it takes to move them
outcome: Restored functional schedule discipline by reshaping team behavior.
core_thesis: A schedule is the visible artifact of an invisible operating model. When a functional organization adopts cross-functional tools, the organization reshapes the tools faster than the tools reshape the organization. Real change comes from moving the team from lightweight coordination to heavyweight ownership; the schedule will follow.
abstract: A coaching engagement at a global semiconductor company on a new-product program for AI data-center customers. The senior project manager left an FTTM workshop with a cross-functional schedule and a heavyweight team structure; three weeks later she had quietly rebuilt that schedule into the functional shape she had used for twenty years. Covers the seven philosophical splits that surfaced, why the pattern is structural rather than personal, and the five-step coaching arc for moving mature PMs from lightweight to heavyweight ownership. Names and sector-identifying details have been removed.

title: Building a $7 billion fab in under two years
subtitle: How an empowered core team and integrated master schedule overcame a two-year projected delay
outcome: Two weeks early on a 2-year mega-fab program, recovering over a year of schedule deficit and avoiding $70M in delay costs.
core_thesis: A two-year deficit doesn't close incrementally. It closes when an empowered core team owns the outcome end-to-end, an integrated master schedule serves as the single source of truth, and refresh planning runs at a cadence frequent enough to expose gaps the same day they appear.
abstract: In 2010, GlobalFoundries set out to build an advanced semiconductor fab in under two years. The site was a 225-acre greenfield in Luther Forest, upstate New York, the budget was $7 billion, and the industry average for a project of this scale was three to four years. lateralworks was engaged to structure the program, build the integrated plan, and drive schedule acceleration using the FTTM framework. The initial macro plan showed the project tracking about two years late. An empowered cross-functional core team, a macro-micro Integrated Master Schedule that grew to over 100,000 tasks, and twice-daily Refresh Planning across 24/7 shifts closed the gap. First qualified silicon came off the production line on December 27, 2011, two weeks ahead of the January 10, 2012 target. The early delivery avoided about $70 million in delay costs. GlobalFoundries adopted the FTTM planning system as the standard for subsequent fab expansions worldwide.

title: Launching Windows CE at startup speed
subtitle: How an empowered product delivery team shipped a first-wave handheld PC in 13 months
outcome: Shipped a first-wave Windows CE handheld PC in 13 months — an 18-month acceleration over a typical Philips program.
core_thesis: When the deadline is existential and the work spans multiple companies, the single most important design decision is organizational, not technical. Stand up a ring-fenced product delivery team with end-to-end ownership, governed above the hierarchy, and let an integrated master schedule do the coordination work that committees do too slowly.
abstract: In 1996, Philips secured a limited exclusivity window to launch Microsoft's Windows CE. lateralworks recommended a ring-fenced Product Delivery Team led by Tony Fadell, with end-to-end ownership reporting above the host hierarchy. A 20-person core team orchestrated 200+ development partners to deliver the Philips Velo in 13 months — an 18-month acceleration over a typical Philips program. The PDT model later became the standard playbook for complex consumer electronics delivery.

title: Charles Schwab IT infrastructure rationalization
subtitle: How program structure and portfolio prioritization halved the path to $15M in annual savings
outcome: Realized $8.8M in annual run-rate savings within 18 months while consolidating the server fleet from 1,100 to 400 — roughly halving the path to projected $15–25M in annual savings.
core_thesis: Time-to-savings programs fail when they lack portfolio prioritization, integrated planning, and financial visibility. lateralworks turned a 400-project backlog into a sequenced, measurable execution engine by applying the same program structuring discipline used in time-to-market product delivery, reframed around cost-savings velocity rather than ship dates.
abstract: Charles Schwab's IT infrastructure rationalization program — migrating 1,100 Solaris/AIX servers and 145 applications to a standardized Linux/Intel platform — was stalling under a 400-project backlog with no prioritization, no integrated plan, and no savings tracking. lateralworks restructured the program around alignment workshops, a six-milestone macro plan, a portfolio prioritization model, and dynamic financial tracking. Within 18 months, the team realized $8.8M in annual run-rate savings, reduced the fleet 64%, and won Schwab's Program of the Year. Independently validated by The Research Board across 22 major enterprises.

title: The 12.12.12 pilot line
subtitle: How Alta Devices recovered an eight-month projected schedule miss and brought the world's most efficient solar cell to manufacturing.
outcome: Pilot line produced first qualified material on the December 12, 2012 funding-gate deadline, closing an eight-month projected schedule gap inside an eleven-month planning window.
core_thesis: A pilot line on a hard deadline cannot be recovered by the departments running its work streams in parallel — recovery requires one integrated schedule, one weekly cadence, and the full management team in the room. On the Alta Devices program, that combination closed an eight-month projected gap inside an eleven-month planning window.
abstract: In late 2011 Alta Devices held the world record for solar-cell efficiency but faced a year-end pilot-line deadline that would gate its next funding round, with the integrated schedule forecasting an eight-month miss. lateralworks rebuilt the program as a single 5,000-activity integrated schedule, restructured the team around lateral deliverables, and ran a weekly pull-in cadence with the full management team. The line produced first qualified material on December 12, 2012 — closing the gap inside an eleven-month planning window.

title: Planning in three days, not three weeks
subtitle: How a chip-development team compressed multi-year program planning from weeks to days, with AI doing 80% of the synthesis and the team scrubbing the rest.
engagement: Multi-year stacked-memory program · three-day planning sprint
outcome: Initial macro plan; program charter, milestone timeline, and macro schedule with gap analysis and core team buy-in in three days against a conventional cycle of three to four weeks.
core_thesis: AI-assisted macro planning compresses about 80% of the synthesis work into hours and routes the remaining 20% — judgment, calibration, local context — through the team. On a multi-year stacked-memory program, that split delivered a publishable charter, milestone matrix, and macro schedule in three days against a conventional cycle of three to four weeks.
abstract: Multi-year program planning conventionally takes weeks of meetings, drafts, and reviews. A semiconductor team replaced that cycle with an AI-assisted three-step flow: milestone timeline, milestone matrix, macro schedule. The AI generated each draft in hours; the team scrubbed and re-prompted. AI did about 80% of the synthesis. The team added the last 20% — judgment, calibration, local context. The first complete plan was on the table in three days. The case documents the flow, the iteration discipline, and nine operating principles.

title: Sony PlayStation
subtitle: The 500K ASIC
outcome: 24-month delivery on a 5× gate-count leap; the engagement roughly doubled LSI Logic in a single year and powered the launch of Sony's first PlayStation.
core_thesis: When a program demands more than the organization can deliver, the response must be structural. Pick one driving customer, integrate hardware and software workstreams under one empowered core team, and run the planning cadence at a frequency that surfaces gaps before they ossify.
abstract: In 1993, Sony entered a console market dominated by Nintendo and Sega with a plan that depended on an unprecedented 500,000-gate single-die ASIC. LSI Logic took the design. lateralworks reframed the program around a single driving customer, stood up the first cross-functional core team in LSI's history, and ran high-frequency refresh planning across hardware and software for two years. Engineering samples shipped 12 months ahead of Sony's schedule. The Sony engagement roughly doubled LSI Logic in a single year.

title: Innovation Accelerated
subtitle: advanced display fab and technology development
outcome: Delivered breakthrough yield, performance, and cycle-time targets on the reset three-year plan, with research-grade process running in production at a fab that did not exist three years earlier.
core_thesis: You cannot accelerate a program you do not see. The first job was making the program visible end-to-end — one integrated plan, one core team, one refresh cycle — and then closing the gap one critical-path week at a time.
abstract: An advanced display device — one of thirty-eight inventions converging on a consumer-product launch — was three programs run as one: a brownfield fab retrofit, a research-to-development process transfer for three color emitters, and a worldwide engineering acceleration to a breakthrough yield target. lateralworks ran the TPM role end-to-end, colocated at the receiving fab for 3+ years. The first deliverable was telling the client the original eighteen-month plan was wrong. The team hit the revised three-year target through COVID.

title: Recovering a worldwide security program
subtitle: How lateralworks recovered Cisco's year-late ACS 5.0 program and protected the hardware roadmap that depended on it
outcome: Brought a year-late, worldwide program back to a converging schedule and shipped ACS 5.0, protecting hundreds of millions in dependent hardware revenue.
core_thesis: A late program rarely recovers because people start working harder. It recovers when the schedule becomes a living instrument the whole team can see and pull on. lateralworks made the gap visible, gave eleven teams ownership of their own end-to-end work, and refreshed and pulled in the plan two and three times a week until the predicted delivery date stopped drifting and started converging on the target.
abstract: Cisco's next-generation access-control platform, ACS 5.0, was running about a year late, and several switching businesses had sequenced dependent hardware behind it. lateralworks installed the FTTM operating system on a live, distributed program — hundreds of engineers, eleven end-to-end teams, multiple continents, one program office. By building one integrated schedule, making the real gap visible, and refreshing and pulling in two to three times a week, the team moved the forecast from open-ended slip to converging delivery. The program shipped, and the roadmap it gated held.

title: One program, many companies
subtitle: Running a multi-site advanced-node development program as a single, integrated team
engagement: Technical program manager — three-year multi-company program
outcome: Called the schedule to the year — five years as assessed, against a two-year client scope and an estimated eight without the integrated program structure.
core_thesis: When a program depends on many companies, the work is not coordination but integration — building one team, one schedule, and one set of decisions out of organizations that arrive as strangers. The integrator's highest-value output is an early, honest read of the two things that bind the schedule: the maturity of what you inherit and the capability of the partners you depend on.
abstract: A Silicon Valley company needed an advanced-node device that worked only in a European research lab to run on a development line it controlled — fast enough to feed a flagship product. lateralworks ran the program as technical program manager, pulling a research institute, a foundry partner, equipment suppliers, and the sponsor into one integrated team. Over three years we retrofitted a fab through lockdown, qualified the line, and transferred the process — and told the sponsor the hard truth in time to act.

title: Integrating a multi-supplier lunar program
subtitle: How lateralworks rebuilt one integrated master schedule and a weekly refresh cadence to put a commercial lunar lander program back on a converging path.
outcome: Replaced disconnected supplier plans with one integrated master schedule refreshed weekly, quantified a 404-day critical-path gap and put it on a converging path, and transferred the scheduling capability to the client's own team.
core_thesis: A hardware program split across many subcontractors distributes the work but holds the integration risk in one place, and status reporting can't force it to converge. Convergence comes from a single integrated master schedule that every supplier's work lives inside, refreshed weekly in one room, with the critical path and the cause of every slip tracked to each target.
abstract: A commercial lunar lander program was running about a year behind its first customer target, its work spread across international subcontractors and its margin already negative. lateralworks replaced the program's disconnected schedules with one integrated master schedule, refreshed weekly in a single room, that re-identified the critical path to every target, recorded the cause of every slip, and drove pull-in actions until the trends turned. A core scheduling capability was seeded and transferred to the client's own managers.

title: Project Rubicon
subtitle: A five-engineer team, a microinverter built into the cable, and a working prototype in under six months
outcome: Reached a field-validated proof of concept in under six months — at about a third of the planned budget and roughly half the typical schedule.
core_thesis: The product a team ships is decided long before the engineering is done — by the conditions leadership sets, the customers the team listens to, and the schedule it runs against. Project Rubicon put five engineers in the right conditions, pointed them at a customer-defined target, and reached a working proof of concept in under six months. The parent company chose not to commercialize it. The method still did exactly what it is built to do.
abstract: A large wire manufacturer asked lateralworks to invest in and run a corporate innovation program: build the solar inverter into the cable itself. lateralworks assembled a five-engineer team, set the host conditions, defined the product with real customers, and drove the work with one integrated schedule. The result was a field-validated proof of concept in under six months — at roughly a third of the planned budget and about half the typical schedule. The parent later chose not to commercialize it; the method still delivered exactly what it was built to do.

title: Project Everest
subtitle: Moving a utility-scale battery maker out of the hardware business, and shipping the first integrated system in twelve months
outcome: Shipped the company's first co-developed system inside the twelve-month target, holding a positive schedule trend against a modeled ~$115K/day cost of delay and recovering the flagship project with no liquidated damages.
core_thesis: A hardware company cannot out-price a commoditized, China-dominated supply chain. It can out-integrate it. Everest moved the client off the factory floor and onto the software and data layer, and proved the move on a single product, on time, with a dedicated team that owned one schedule end to end.
abstract: A Western utility-scale battery maker was losing an unwinnable price war against China-dominated hardware. lateralworks repositioned the company from hardware manufacturer to systems integrator and data business, then proved the model on Everest — its first co-developed, roughly 5 MWh system, with hardware from China and Korea, external firmware, and an internal software stack fused into one certified product. A dedicated heavyweight core team ran firmware and software on one critical path with a weekly cost-of-delay cadence, releasing inside the twelve-month target. Client-identifying details removed.

title: Lab realignment
subtitle: How Applied Materials collapsed four labs into two and hit a $20M-a-year savings target on schedule — without ever stopping the business.
outcome: $20M-a-year savings target met on schedule — 60+ tools relocated and requalified in 18 months with zero interruption to the running business.
core_thesis: The savings were never in doubt; the schedule was. Every quarter of delay cost Applied roughly $5M it would never recover, so lateralworks structured the program so the schedule itself protected the money — built around tools rather than buildings, driven by one repeatable move template, and refreshed weekly so slips surfaced as trends before they became misses.
abstract: Applied Materials set out to consolidate its process and demonstration labs from four buildings into two — a permanent $20M-a-year cost reduction, blocked by the fact that the labs could not close. More than sixty truck-sized tools running customer demos, low-volume production, and active development had to move in eighteen months. lateralworks built the schedule around tools and tool farms rather than buildings, templated the move once, and drove the program with weekly refresh planning. The program finished on schedule, and the business never stopped.

title: Prioritizing through the crash
subtitle: Portfolio modeling and project selection at Applied Materials, 2007–2009
outcome: Reprioritized a 73-program portfolio in three weeks after Lehman failed, giving AGS a ranked, defensible basis for the November 2008 cost reduction.
core_thesis: A project portfolio is a standing decision about where scarce resources go. The organizations that navigate downturns best are the ones whose planning survives contact with bad times. A portfolio built on an explicit decision model can be re-run in weeks when the world changes. A portfolio built on accumulated commitments cannot.
abstract: Between 2007 and 2009, lateralworks helped two of Applied Materials' largest organizations turn hundreds of programs into ranked, executable portfolios using AHP decision modeling — the fastDecision toolset now shipped as fastDecisionAI. In Global Operations, the model quantified the gap between effort and value: the top two initiatives carried 64 percent of the benefit while a fourth-ranked initiative absorbed outsized energy. When Lehman failed six days after the AGS three-year plan was set, the rebuilt model ranked all 73 programs against recession-weighted criteria in three weeks.

title: Six competitors, one schedule
subtitle: How a six-company consortium developed the 20nm process node as a single program — and took three years out of the development schedule
outcome: Initial 20nm process and design methods transferred to all six partners in 24 months — three years out of the five-year baseline the macro plan exposed.
core_thesis: Invention does not have to arrive on its own clock. When the learning cycles that produce it are named, scheduled, resourced, and run concurrently — and when one person owns each decision — a research program behaves like a delivery program. That is managed innovation: scheduled invention. On 20nm it was worth three years.
abstract: In 2010, six semiconductor companies — IBM, GlobalFoundries, Samsung, STMicroelectronics, Infineon, and Chartered — were jointly developing the 20nm node at East Fishkill with no single point of decision. GlobalFoundries engaged lateralworks as program integrator. We formed one core team with a single product boss, built the program's first honest macro plan — which showed five years of work against the two-year target — then attacked the learning rate. The process transferred to every partner in 24 months.

title: The product they thought they knew
subtitle: How a utility-scale energy storage integrator used Voice of the Customer to redefine its next-generation platform — and found its customers valued something else entirely
engagement: VOC study and next-generation product definition, 2024
outcome: Overturned two load-bearing product assumptions before development capital was committed, redirecting the next-generation program to an availability-first, software-core product definition.
core_thesis: Everest’s internal product concept was coherent, technically sophisticated, and wrong in two of its central assumptions. A VOC council, structured discovery, and AHP pairwise prioritization let customers re-rank the company’s priorities before the capital was committed — and revealed that in a deflating hardware market, the differentiated product is availability itself, delivered and proven by software.
abstract: A global integrator of utility-scale battery energy storage set out to define its next-generation product around higher density, duration flexibility, and lower price. A structured VOC program — council of developers, IPPs, a utility, owner-operators, and contractors, run through discovery interviews, surveys, and AHP pairwise workshops — showed customers weighted lifetime power and energy availability, delivered and proven by software. The program was redirected: hardware cost-down protecting TCO drivers, availability as the engineering agenda, software elevated to product core. Client anonymized.

title: 100,000 activities, one critical path
subtitle: How the macro-micro roll-up in fastProjectAI let a $7 billion greenfield fab run eight independent module schedules — and still read a single end-to-end program critical path
engagement: Greenfield fab schedule architecture and program roll-up, 2009–2011
outcome: First silicon two weeks ahead of schedule on a program costing delay at roughly $5M a day — on the order of $70M — with the Fab8 roll-up code later productized as the Macro-Micro Roll-up in fastProjectAI.
core_thesis: A program of 100,000 activities cannot be read in one schedule, and it cannot be run in fifty disconnected ones. The macro-micro roll-up keeps every schedule small enough for one team to own, and connected enough that a single critical path runs from the first procurement task to first silicon.
abstract: The $7 billion Fab8 greenfield fab in Malta, New York needed more than 100,000 activities to reach first silicon — too big for one schedule, too interconnected for many. lateralworks resolved the dilemma with the macro-micro architecture: one cross-functional macro-schedule, eight module-owned micro-schedules, synchronized twice a day by custom roll-up code that rebuilt the macro as a live critical-path model rather than a status report. Fab8 delivered first silicon two weeks early; the machinery became the Macro-Micro Roll-up in fastProjectAI.

title: Tilting the organization on its side
subtitle: How a functional semiconductor company rebuilt four first-of-a-kind programs around heavyweight product delivery teams — and what it took to get its new leaders to lead
engagement: Heavyweight PDT operating model and leadership development, 2026 (live engagement)
outcome: Role charters with explicit freedom levels issued across all four programs; weekly schedule refresh standing across all four teams; research-grade problems isolated into dedicated tiger teams; monthly general-manager walk-through cadence launched.
core_thesis: A functional organization becomes fast when it tilts on its side: when a dedicated team owns each product end to end and the functions provision that team instead of directing it. The org chart is the easy part. The hard part is that the new structure asks people to lead in ways their careers never taught them — and until leadership behavior catches up with structural authority, the tilt exists only on paper.
abstract: A global semiconductor company set out to win four first-of-a-kind power products for AI data centers — each on a compressed schedule, each carrying research-grade technical risk. Working with lateralworks, it redesigned the programs around heavyweight product delivery teams: dedicated cross-functional core teams led by a product delivery leader paired with a program manager, with decision authority made explicit through freedom-scale tables. Then came the real problem: the newly named leaders, capable managers with careers formed inside functional silos, did not lead. This case examines why that gap is the predictable cost of the tilt, and what closed it — written role charters, the CEO/COO pairing, honest schedules that plan learning cycles, tiger teams for the hard 10%, and a general manager armed to demand reality instead of reassurance.

title: Three teams, three breakthroughs
subtitle: How the challenge process found technical and schedule breakthroughs inside three storage development programs
engagement: Challenge process workshops across three development programs, 2014–2015
outcome: A modeled fifteen-month roadmap acceleration on one program, three- and four-month deliverable pull-ins on a second, and a doubled learning rate on a third — with no added headcount and no relaxed requirements.
core_thesis: A schedule gap is not evidence that requirements must be relaxed. Treated correctly, the gap is raw material: the pressure that forces a team to surface its assumptions, challenge them one by one, and discover ways of working it had quietly classified as impossible.
abstract: In 2014 a major disk-drive storage company had three critical programs trending late at once — one roughly ten months behind, one three months late and drifting, one slipping progressively on a plan that assumed its experiments would work the first time. Each team was taken offsite for a one-day challenge workshop: surface the assumptions, ask why each is believed, generate alternatives with the constraints switched off, and act within seven days. The results: a roadmap rebuilt in a week around a modeled fifteen-month pull-in, a headline technology removed because it was desired but not required, and an experiment plan restructured to learn twice as fast — without de-featuring a single product.
